families.s: HSE surface-engineering toxic-metal and sensitiser exposure guidance
families.t: cyanides, dichromate, chromium trioxide, nickel, isocyanate paints, toxic inventory, tanks, fume, asthma, dermatitis and emergency control
f: Surface-engineering sites may hold cyanides, dichromate and chromium trioxide in raw material, process tanks or waste.
These substances can present serious toxic and respiratory hazards.
Two-pack isocyanate paints can cause occupational asthma and dermatitis.
Isocyanates are a major cause of occupational asthma in spraying work.
Tanks, additions, transfers and waste handling should minimise splash, mist and fume.
Local exhaust ventilation should capture airborne contaminants near the source.
Chemical compatibility, segregation and emergency arrangements should reflect the substances held.
Exposure monitoring, health surveillance and maintenance should verify continuing control.
families.g: Toxic surface-engineering risk depends on metal and chemical species, concentration and inventory, tank and transfer design, mist and fume generation, ventilation, skin contact, waste, monitoring and emergency response.

families.s: HSE circular-saw bench guarding and kickback-prevention guidance
families.t: blade contact, ejection, riving knife, top guard, fence, take-off table, push sticks, braking, dust and fire
f: Circular-saw benches present blade-contact and workpiece-ejection hazards.
A riving knife should be fitted and adjusted close to the blade.
The riving knife should suit the blade plate and kerf dimensions.
The top guard should cover the exposed blade and tooth gullets as far as practicable.
Fence position should reduce trapping and kickback risk.
Take-off support should prevent workers reaching near the blade to collect work.
Push sticks or other aids should keep hands away for small or narrow work.
Dust extraction and ignition control are needed because wood dust can create fire and explosion risk.
families.g: Circular-saw risk depends on blade and tooling, riving knife and guard adjustment, fence and support, workpiece size and condition, feed method, braking, dust extraction, housekeeping and operator competence.

families.s: HSE dimension and panel-saw blade, guard and kickback guidance
families.t: ripping, cross-cutting, grooving, scribing blade, blade selection, top guard, positive hook, feather boards, ejection and work support
f: Dimension saws can be used for ripping, cross-cutting and grooving.
The correct blade should be selected for the cutting mode.
A scribing blade may be used with the main blade to control splintering on coated materials.
The guard should cover both blades when they are in use.
A positive-hook blade used for cross-cutting can pull material into the blade and create run-away risk.
Feather boards and suitable supports can reduce kickback during grooving or rebating.
The machine and task should be included in a workshop risk assessment.
Training and supervision should address each operating mode, blade change and setup.
families.g: Panel-saw risk depends on cutting mode and blade, guard and scribing arrangement, workpiece and support, fence and feather boards, kickback and ejection, setup, braking and competence.

families.s: HSE cross-cut saw guarding, return-device and hand-exclusion guidance
families.t: blade guard, brake or return device, protected rest position, no-go zone, table edge, jigs, off-cuts, push sticks and riving knife
f: Cross-cut saw guards should cover as much of the blade as possible.
The saw should have a brake or a device that returns the cutting head to a protected position.
A hand no-go area should be maintained on both sides of the blade.
The cut should finish before the blade reaches the table edge and operator body.
Stake pointing requires a properly designed jig and adequate support.
Sharp off-cuts should be removed regularly so they cannot jam or be ejected.
A push stick or stopped machine should be used when removing hazardous off-cuts.
A riving knife is required if the saw is also used for ripping.
families.g: Cross-cut saw risk depends on blade and guard, return and braking, hand position and table geometry, work support and jigs, off-cut accumulation, cutting mode, housekeeping and competence.

families.s: HSE hand-fed planer, spindle-moulder and sander safeguarding guidance
families.t: cutter contact, kickback, bridge and tunnel guards, push blocks, tooling, power feed, ejection, table adjustment, braking and training
f: Surface planers can pull fingers toward exposed cutters after kickback.
Bridge or tunnel guards should expose only the minimum cutter area required.
Push blocks should be used for small workpieces on planers.
Vertical spindle moulders present cutter-contact and workpiece or tooling-ejection hazards.
Tunnel guards, jigs, stop blocks and power feed can reduce access and ejection risk.
Disc, bobbin and belt sanders require close table or adjustable guards and controlled work positioning.
Braking, suitable tooling and planned maintenance support safe stopping and operation.
Machine-specific assessment, instruction, training and supervision are required for high-risk hand-fed woodworking machines.
families.g: Hand-fed woodworking-machine risk depends on cutter or abrasive, guard adjustment, tooling and workpiece, kickback and ejection, jigs and power feed, braking, dust extraction, maintenance and competence.
